title: Death may come first
hookLine: a half-written apology in your versions; Shantideva says don't count on later
tomorrow: you leave it all behind. so why fight over any of it?

cards: There's a message sitting in a lot of versions folders. It starts with I'm sorry, and stops halfway through the second line.

The plan is to finish it when the moment is right: when things calm down, when they bring it up first, when the words come out better. The moment keeps not arriving. So yesterday's question: why not fix it later?
Shantideva's reason fits in one blunt line.

teach.h: DEATH MAY COME BEFORE IT'S MENDED.
teach.b: Still inside his confession, after taking refuge, he says it plainly: death may come before my wrongs are mended.

teach.h: IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR THE JOB.
teach.b: Death doesn't wait to see whether the job is done. Sick or healthy, he says, this life can't be trusted to last. It sounds grim, and he means it seriously.
But read where it sits. It isn't there to frighten anyone into a corner.

teach.h: THE REASON UNDER THE WHOLE WEEK.
teach.b: It's the reason under everything this week. Hard to find: so use it. Lightning: so look while it flashes.
Wish, then go: so don't stop at the map. And now the plainest version: whatever needs mending, the mending has a clock on it, and nobody can see the clock. Shantideva's answer isn't panic.
It's a short list of things worth doing today instead of someday. The apology. The call.
The thing you owe someone, said straight.

how: Reflection on death is part of practice across Buddhist schools; many teachers pair it with the precious human life, as a reason to act well now rather than as a cause for fear.

games.q: what does “death may come first” mean?
o: a belief that bad deeds will bring an early death
a reason to mend things today instead of someday
a warning that only the very old need to prepare

games.q: the week, by its lines — tap the pairs.
p: the blind turtle and the yoke
a good thought, brief but clear
so the mending belongs to today

s: Shantideva brings up death to make readers panic
it's a reason to act: the mending has a clock on it, so do it today.
he says death doesn't wait to see whether the job is done
sick or healthy, he says, this life can't be trusted to last.
the best apology waits for the perfect moment
the moment keeps not arriving. Shantideva's line is mend it now.

games.q: you snapped at your dad this morning and left for work. he hasn't texted. what fits Shantideva's line?
o: wait until dinner, when you can say it properly in person.
text him now: sorry about this morning, i'll explain later.
let it go; he probably forgot about it already.
games.why: a short mend now beats a perfect one later. death may come first, so the mending belongs to today.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that needs mending: a word, a debt, a silence. Name what's been in the way. Then decide exactly when you'll do it, today, down to the hour, and see yourself doing it.
Rest in that plan for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Death may come first: Shantideva's reason not to wait. It may arrive before a wrong is mended, so the mending belongs to today.

orig.note: Sanskrit: death. In chapter two Shantideva warns that it may come before his wrongs are mended.

carryVoice: For the road: mend it now, while the door is still open. A week of the poem, done.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 2.32-2.33 (death may come before my wrongs are mended; it does not wait for what is done or undone)
